name: Sun avoidance / hat protocol

lead: Sun avoidance means limiting UV exposure through shade, timing and physical barriers like wide-brimmed hats, usually alongside sunscreen. It is most associated with managing melasma and slowing photoageing.
Dermatology sources describe sun as a main trigger of melasma and the main external driver of skin ageing, but no trials test a hat protocol specifically.

paras: Physical barriers block UV and visible light before they reach the skin, which sources say can stimulate pigment-producing cells and drive photoageing.
Few direct risks are reported. Reviews discuss whether strict avoidance affects vitamin D status, while Wikipedia notes diet and supplements can supply it.

lead: Sun avoidance, often paired with wide-brimmed hats, is a skincare practice in which people minimise ultraviolet (UV) and sometimes visible-light exposure to the face, most commonly to prevent or control melasma and to slow visible skin ageing. It goes beyond routine sunscreen use to include staying in shade, avoiding midday sun, and wearing hats, sunglasses and protective clothing.

Dermatology sources describe sun exposure as a main trigger of melasma and as the primary external cause of skin ageing [1][2]. Wikipedia's melasma article states that strict sun avoidance is needed for treatment to work and that even small amounts of sun can bring back faded patches [3]. Sunscreen references describe sunscreen as a supplement to hats, sunglasses and protective clothing [4]. No clinical trial of a hat-specific protocol appears in the sources consulted.
infobox: Prevent melasma recurrence, slow photoageing, reduce skin cancer risk
Wide-brimmed hats, shade, sunscreen, UPF clothing, sunglasses

paras: The practice combines behavioural measures (seeking shade, avoiding peak sun hours, limiting outdoor time) with physical barriers such as brimmed hats and UPF-rated clothing, usually alongside broad-spectrum sunscreen. Wikipedia describes sunscreen as one part of a wider set of measures that includes sunhats, sunglasses, protective clothing and umbrellas, and notes that fabric UPF ratings work similarly to SPF [4].

Melasma is a chronic, relapsing pigmentation disorder. Wikipedia reports that UVA, UVB and visible light can all stimulate pigment production, that recurrence is common in summer, and that strict sun avoidance is required for treatment to succeed [3]. Mineral sunscreens containing zinc oxide or titanium dioxide are described as preferred for this reason [3].

Photoageing reviews describe chronic sun exposure as the main external cause of skin ageing, which is the other common motive for the practice [2]. Epidemiological reviews link UV exposure to melanoma and to basal and squamous cell carcinomas [5][6]. A modelling study from 1986 estimated that regular sunscreen use in the first 18 years of life could substantially lower lifetime nonmelanoma skin cancer incidence [6].

No studies found of a combined sun-avoidance and hat protocol as such. Related evidence concerns sunscreen: a 2013 Australian trial of about 900 people reported smoother, more resilient skin after 4.5 years of daily sunscreen use, according to Wikipedia's summary [4]. The 1986 modelling study above is an estimate, not a trial [6].

Skin is a major source of vitamin D, and reviews have discussed how much sun exposure is needed for adequate vitamin D status and whether strict avoidance may lower it [7][8]. Wikipedia states that typical sunscreen use usually does not cause deficiency, and that diet and supplements can supply vitamin D [4]. Ecological analyses have also reported associations between lower solar UVB and higher mortality from some cancers, though such analyses cannot establish cause [9].

Proponents treat strict sun avoidance as a foundation of long-term facial appearance, aimed at preventing pigmentation, wrinkles and uneven tone. The practice is also discussed among people managing melasma, where dermatology sources similarly emphasise sun protection [3].

lore.intro: Sun avoidance is discussed as a baseline habit for skin quality, often as an add-on to sunscreen.
